extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students and instructors using Rudin's Principles of Mathematical Analysis
extracted.subtask_description: A collection of supplemental exercises, annotations, and instructor/student guidance for Chapters 1–7 of Rudin's Principles of Mathematical Analysis, including exercise titles, difficulty estimates, dependency notes, and comments/hints for solving and assigning problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulty codes (d:1 to d:5)
rubrics_metrics.description: My estimate of the difficulty of each exercise is shown by a code d: 1 to d: 5. Codes d: 1 to d: 3 indicate exercises that it would be appropriate to assign in a non-honors class as 'easier', 'typical', and 'more difficult' problems; d: 2 to d: 4 would have the same roles in an honors course, while d: 5 indicates the sort of exercise that might be used as an extra-credit 'challenge problem' in an honors course.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these codes to choose problems appropriate to course level: d:1–3 for non-honors assignments, d:2–4 for honors, and d:5 for challenge/extra-credit. Treat these estimates as fallible: the author cautions not to put too much faith in them and notes subjective inconsistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multi-part difficulty notation
rubrics_metrics.description: If an exercise consists of several parts of notably different difficulties, I may write something like d: 2, 2, 4 to indicate that parts (a) and (b) have difficulty 2, while part (c) has difficulty 4.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assigning or grading multi-part exercises, respect per-part difficulty distinctions; you may assign different weights/points per part accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between difficulty and amount of work
rubrics_metrics.description: The difficulty of an exercise is not the same as the amount of work it involves – a long series of straightforward manipulations can have a low level of difficulty, but involve a lot of work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not equate 'hard' with 'time-consuming'. Consider both difficulty and expected time when assigning problems; the author attempted to quantify workload separately (see scoring/pointing guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Desire to assign point-values to calibrate workload
rubrics_metrics.description: I would like to similarly assign point-values to each exercise here, from which it should be possible to similarly calibrate assignments. But I don’t have the time to do this at present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested method (from author's grading experience): list the steps you expect in a solution, assign points per step (including half/1.5 points for tiny/complex steps), and choose total points per homework to target desired student time (example: 25-point assignment kept weekly time near ~13 hours/week).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependencies notation ('>') and dependency notes
rubrics_metrics.description: After the title and difficulty-code, I note in some cases that the exercise depends on some other exercise, writing '>' to mean 'must be done after ...'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use '>' annotations to indicate prerequisite exercises or results; instructors should respect these when sequencing assignments. The author also recommends reverse-dependency notes (marking exercises which later exercises depend on) to aid assignment planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: True/False questions (numbered '0') and role
rubrics_metrics.description: In most sections (starting with §1.2) the exercises I give begin with one numbered '0', and consisting of one or more True/False questions, with answers shown at the bottom of the next page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are intended to check elementary understanding and awareness (e.g., difference between statement and converse, order of quantification, what counterexamples show). No difficulty-codes are given; in theory they should be 'd:0' and require no original thought, though occasionally they test slightly nontrivial applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solutions must contain proofs (unless stated otherwise)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless the contrary is stated, solutions to homework problems are expected to contain proofs, even if the problems are not so worded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affirmative answers require proofs that the statement is always true; negative answers require explicit counterexamples satisfying all hypotheses except the deleted one when asked to show failure upon deletion of a condition. True/False self-checks should be justifiable by proof/counterexample when not simply restatements from the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advice on approaching problems (definitions → theorems → adaptations)
rubrics_metrics.description: An exercise may only require you to use the definitions in the relevant section of Rudin, or it may require for its proof some results proved there, or an argument using the same method of proof as some result proved there. So in approaching each problem, first see whether the result becomes reasonably straightforward when all the relevant definitions are noted, and also ask yourself whether the statement you are to prove is related to the conclusion of any of the theorems in the section, and if so, whether that theorem can be applied as it stands, or whether a modification of the proof can give the result you need.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematic approach: (1) write down relevant definitions; (2) scan nearby theorems for related conclusions; (3) try direct application or a modification of a known proof; (4) check whether earlier sections supply needed tools (some exercises may legitimately depend on earlier material).

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy on using results from other courses
rubrics_metrics.description: From time to time students in the class ask 'Can we use results from other courses in our homework?' The answer is, in general, 'No.' Rudin shows how the material of lower division calculus can be developed, essentially from scratch, in a rigorous fashion. Hence to call on material you have seen developed in the loose fashion of your earlier courses would defeat the purpose. Of course, there are certain compromises: As Rudin says, he will assume the basic properties of integers and rational numbers, so you have to do so too. Moreover, once one has developed rigorously the familiar laws of differentiation and integration (a minor aspect of the material of this course), the application of these is not essentially different from what you learned in calculus, so it is probably not essential to state explicitly in homework for later sections which of those laws you are using at every step. When in doubt on such matters, ask your instructor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on unproven-calculus-level heuristics; allowed exceptions: basic integer/rational properties and standard calculus laws once developed in-course. Ask instructor when unsure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notation and terminology adherence
rubrics_metrics.description: I have followed Rudin’s notation and terminology very closely, e.g. using R for the field of real numbers, J for the set of positive integers, and 'at most countable' to describe a set of cardinality ≤ ℵ0. But on a few points I have diverged from his notation: I distinguish between sequences and sets, and I use ⊆ rather than ⊂ for inclusion. I also occasionally use the symbols ∀ and ∃.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible follow Rudin's notation for consistency; author notes divergences explicitly — be aware of them when solving/communicating solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numbering and classification of exercises to guide assignment timing
rubrics_metrics.description: I have given numbers to the sections in each chapter of Rudin, in general taking each of his capitalized headings to begin a new numbered section... My exercises are referred to by boldfaced symbols showing the chapter and section, followed by a colon and an exercise-number; e.g., under section 1.4 you will find Exercises 1.4:1, 1.4:2, etc. Rudin puts his exercises at the ends of the chapters; in these notes I abbreviate 'Chapter M, Rudin’s Exercise N' to M : R N. However, I list both my exercises and his under the relevant section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The sectional listing is intended to show students/instructors which exercises are appropriate to attempt or assign after a given section has been covered. Use the section mapping to choose timely problems; avoid assigning exercises before prerequisite sections are taught (see dependency notes).

rubrics_metrics.name: True/False question design goals
rubrics_metrics.description: I tried to write them to check for the most elementary things that students typically get confused on, such as the difference between a statement and its converse, and order of quantification, and for the awareness of what Rudin’s various counterexamples show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use True/False items as quick comprehension checks rather than proof exercises; they help ensure students have internalized definitions and common pitfalls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annotate exercises that require earlier material or different section placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Some exercises belong under a different section strictly speaking, since one needs the tools in that section to do it. Thus, such exercises should not be assigned to be done before students have read the required sections, and students working it may assume that Q has the properties of an ordered field as described in that section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing or assigning exercises, explicitly annotate if an exercise uses material from other sections and avoid premature assignment; students may assume listed prerequisites when working those annotated problems.
